usage: with 좋다 use the subject particle 가, not 를: 점수가 좋다, never 점수를 좋다
when an action verb like 받다 acts on it, the object particle 를 returns
나오다 is intransitive, so the score is the subject (가), not the object
Koreans pair a score with 높다/낮다 (high/low), never 크다/작다 (big/small)
examples: 점수가 좋아요.
The score is good.
The simplest frame: just the noun plus 가 and an adjective, the everyday way to comment on a result.
저는 한국어 시험 점수를 받았어요.
I got my Korean test score back.
받다 takes 를 because you actively receive the number that was handed to you.
선생님, 제 점수가 왜 이렇게 낮아요?
Teacher, why is my score so low?
A real classroom complaint: 낮다 (low) is the natural opposite of 높다, never 작다.
nuance: 점수 is the numeric points you earn on a test, quiz, or game — the raw figure itself, written 95점 with the counter 점. The hanja is 點數, literally 'dot-number', from 點 (point/dot) plus 數 (number), so it is intrinsically a counted quantity. Do not confuse it with its near-synonym 성적 (成績): 성적 is your broader academic standing or report-card record (overall grades, ranking, a transcript), while 점수 is one concrete number on one item — you can have a good 점수 on a single quiz yet a poor overall 성적. The natural verbs are 점수가 나오다 (the score comes out / is released) and 점수를 받다 (to receive a score); for high or low you must say 점수가 높다/낮다, NOT 크다/작다. The English-speaker trap is the particle: with the descriptive 좋다/높다 the score is the subject and takes 가 (점수가 좋다), so saying 점수를 좋다 by copying English 'I scored a good score' is ungrammatical.

usage: 펴다 (spread open) is the standard classroom verb for opening a book to a page, not 열다
나오다 with 에 is how Koreans say content 'comes up' in a book
로 marks the textbook as the tool/means you study by
a subject name directly modifies 교과서 with no particle between them
examples: 교과서를 펴세요.
Please open your textbook.
The exact phrase a teacher says: 펴다 plus the polite command -세요.
답이 교과서에 다 나와 있어요.
The answers are all right there in the textbook.
에 marks the book as the location where the answers appear (나와 있다).
저는 인터넷 강의보다 교과서로 공부하는 게 편해요.
I find studying with the textbook easier than online lectures.
로 frames the textbook as the means, contrasted with 강의 via 보다.
nuance: 교과서 is the official course book for a specific school subject — the authorized text a class is taught from, often government-approved (국정/검정 교과서). The hanja 敎科書 breaks down as 敎 (teach) + 科 (subject/branch) + 書 (book), literally 'teaching-subject book', which is exactly its job. Keep three near-words apart: a 공책 (空冊, 'empty book') is a blank notebook you write in; a 참고서 (參考書) is a supplementary study/reference guide; and a plain 책 is any book at all — only 교과서 is the core subject text used in lessons. The natural verb is 교과서를 펴다 (open it to a page) rather than 열다 (which suits a door or lid), and you study 교과서로 (by means of the textbook). The English-speaker pitfall is calling any school book a 책 or mixing it with 공책: if you say 교과서에 써요 meaning you write in it, a Korean pictures defacing the printed text — you write 공책에, in your notebook, not in the 교과서.

usage: put it in the pencil case
넣다 (put in) naturally pairs with 에 to mark where something goes
existence/possession uses 있다 with the subject particle 이
unlike a book, a case has a lid, so 열다 (open) is correct here
filled pencil cases are typically described with 귀엽다 (cute) by students
examples: 필통이 책상 위에 있어요.
The pencil case is on the desk.
A simple location statement: 위에 (on top) plus 있어요 for where it sits.
연필을 필통에 넣어요.
I put the pencil into the pencil case.
에 marks the destination of 넣다; the pencil (object) takes 를.
새 필통을 샀는데 연필이랑 지우개가 안 들어가요.
I bought a new pencil case but the pencil and eraser don't fit.
A real-life grumble: 들어가다 (to fit inside) with the negative 안.
nuance: 필통 is the small case or box that holds your writing implements — pens, pencils, eraser. The word is Sino-Korean 筆筒, from 筆 (writing brush/pen) + 筒 (tube/cylinder), originally a 'brush-tube', a holder for calligraphy brushes that now means any pencil case. Do not confuse the container with its contents: 연필 (鉛筆, 'lead-brush') is the pencil itself, 볼펜 a ballpoint, and 지우개 the eraser — the 필통 is merely the case they live in. Because a case has a lid you 필통을 열다 (open it) and you 연필을 필통에 넣다 (put a pencil in), so the location particle 에 marks where things go. The English-speaker pitfall is naming the part for the whole: a beginner may point at a pencil and say 필통, but 필통 is strictly the case — if you mean the pencil, say 연필. Also avoid the verb 입다/신다 here; you do not 'wear' a 필통, you 열다 it or 가지고 다니다 (carry it around).

Saying 필통에 연필이 있다 when you mean to put it in, then using 있다 instead of 넣다. 있다 states it is already there; the action of inserting is 넣다 (필통에 넣어요).

usage: carry the school bag (on the back)
메다 is the dedicated verb for shouldering a backpack, not 들다 or 입다
put it in the school bag
에 marks the bag as the place something goes into with 넣다
책가방 is habitually described as 무겁다 (heavy) because of the books inside
싸다 (to pack/wrap) is how Koreans say they get their bag ready
examples: 책가방이 무거워요.
The school bag is heavy.
The basic complaint frame: subject plus the adjective 무겁다.
교과서를 책가방에 넣었어요.
I put the textbook into my school bag.
에 marks where the textbook goes; 넣다 is the action of putting in.
아침마다 책가방을 메고 학교에 가요.
Every morning I put my bag on my back and head to school.
메고 (shouldering, and then…) chains the bag onto the going; -고 links the two actions.
nuance: 책가방 is the bag a student carries books and supplies in — in practice a backpack worn on both shoulders. It is a compound of 책 (冊, book, Sino-Korean) + 가방 (bag, a native-feeling loanword), literally 'book-bag'. The crucial point is the verb: a backpack worn on the back/shoulder takes 메다 (책가방을 메다), whereas a handbag or briefcase carried in the hand takes 들다 (가방을 들다) — choosing the wrong one sounds off, like saying you 'hold' a backpack in your fist. You also 책가방을 싸다 (pack it) the night before and 책가방에 넣다 (put things in). Its near-words: a generic 가방 is any bag, a 백팩 is the English loan 'backpack', and a 핸드백 is a woman's handbag — 책가방 specifically frames it by its school-book purpose. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 입다 (wear) or 들다 (hold) because English says 'wear a backpack' or 'carry a bag'; in Korean a backpack is neither worn like clothes nor held like a purse — it is 메다, shouldered.

usage: 활동(놀다) happens AT a place, so the action particle 에서 is required
모이다 marks the field as the end point of movement, so 에
a 운동장 is rated by area with 넓다 (spacious), not 크다
run a lap around the field
돌다 with 을 treats the track as the path you traverse
examples: 운동장이 넓어요.
The playground is spacious.
A first sentence: subject 가 plus 넓다, the standard way to size up an area.
학생들이 운동장에서 축구를 해요.
The students play soccer on the field.
에서 because 축구를 하다 (the activity) happens there; the place hosts an action.
체육 시간에 운동장에 나가서 줄을 섰어요.
In PE class we went out to the field and lined up.
에 marks the destination of 나가다 (go out to); then 줄을 서다 (line up) follows.
nuance: 운동장 is the open sports field or grounds of a school where pupils exercise, run, and play — typically a large dirt or turf area with a track, the heart of Korean school PE and 체육대회 (sports day). The hanja is 運動場: 運 (move) + 動 (move) — together 運動 means 'exercise/sports' — plus 場 (place/ground), so the whole is literally 'exercise-grounds'. The make-or-break grammar is 에서 vs 에: use 에서 for what you DO there (운동장에서 뛰다/놀다/축구하다), because 에서 marks the location of an action, but use 에 only for motion toward it (운동장에 가다/나가다/모이다). Its near-word 놀이터 is the little playground with swings and a slide for small children, whereas 운동장 is the big school athletic field — do not mix them. Size is 넓다 (spacious), not 크다. The English-speaker pitfall is using a single 'at' particle for everything: English 'play at the playground' and 'go to the playground' both feel like one preposition, but Korean splits them — 운동장에서 놀다 (play, action) yet 운동장에 가다 (go, destination), and putting 에 where an activity happens (운동장에 놀아요) is a classic error.

Confusing 운동장 with 놀이터. 놀이터 is a small children's playground with swings; the school sports field is 운동장. A high-schooler plays soccer on the 운동장, not the 놀이터.
Describing the field as 커요. Area is judged by spaciousness, so the natural adjective is 넓다: 운동장이 넓어요.

usage: meet in front of the gate
교문 앞 (gate-front) is the usual meeting spot; 에서 marks where you meet
지나다 (pass) takes 을, treating the gate as the point you go past
닫히다 (be closed) is the verb for a gate shutting at curfew time
앞 (front) attaches to 교문 to pinpoint the area before it
examples: 교문이 커요.
The school gate is big.
Plain description: 교문 as subject with 크다, fine for a physical structure's size.
친구를 교문 앞에서 만났어요.
I met my friend in front of the school gate.
에서 marks the spot of the meeting; 교문 앞 is the conventional rendezvous point.
지각해서 교문이 닫히기 전에 뛰어 들어갔어요.
I was running late, so I dashed in before the gate closed.
닫히기 전에 (before it closes) plus 뛰어 들어가다 (run in) — the real drama of a tardy student.
nuance: 교문 is the main gate at the entrance of a school — the formal threshold students pass through each day, often guarded and shut after the bell. The hanja 校門 is 校 (school) + 門 (gate/door), literally 'school-gate'. Distinguish it from the broader 정문 (正門, 'main/front gate' of any building or institution) and from a plain 문 (any door): 교문 specifically frames the gate as a school's, so a hospital's main entrance is its 정문, not its 교문. Note that 門 in Korea names large gates and named structures (광화문 Gwanghwamun, 동대문 Dongdaemun), so 교문 carries that weightier 'gateway' feel, not a flimsy door. The natural collocations are 교문 앞에서 만나다 (meet in front of the gate — the default student meetup) and 교문을 지나다 (pass through it), and a gate 닫히다 (closes) at curfew. Unlike a sports field judged by 넓다, a gate's size is 크다. The English-speaker pitfall is over-generalizing 'gate/door' to plain 문 — 문을 지나다 sounds like passing some random door; for the school's entrance gate you want 교문을 지나다.

Marking the meeting place with 에 instead of 에서. Meeting is an action, so the place takes 에서: 교문 앞에서 만나요, not 교문 앞에 만나요.

usage: 입다 is the verb for putting on upper-body/whole clothing, which a uniform is
어울리다 (to suit) with 가 is how Koreans compliment how clothes look on someone
맞추다 means to have clothes custom-made to your size, common for new uniforms
교복 is typically bought new (새) at the start of a school year
examples: 교복이 예뻐요.
The uniform is pretty.
Simple appraisal: subject 가 plus 예쁘다, the everyday way to praise its looks.
저는 매일 교복을 입고 학교에 가요.
I wear my uniform to school every day.
입고 (wearing, and then…) links dressing to going via -고; 를 marks the uniform.
교복 치마가 너무 짧아서 좀 불편해요.
The uniform skirt is so short it's a bit uncomfortable.
A real student remark: 치마 (skirt) as a part of the 교복, with 짧다 (short).
nuance: 교복 is the prescribed uniform students wear at a Korean middle or high school — a recognizable set (blazer, shirt, skirt or trousers, often a name tag) that signals which school you attend. The hanja 校服 is 校 (school) + 服 (clothes/garment), literally 'school-clothes'. The 服 element appears in many clothing words — 한복 (Korean dress), 양복 (a Western suit), 교복 — so it reliably means 'attire'. Crucially the verb is 입다 (입다 covers shirts, jackets, dresses, and uniforms — anything worn on the torso or as a full outfit), NOT 신다 (which is only for footwear) and NOT 쓰다 (for hats/glasses): you 교복을 입다. Other natural phrases are 교복을 맞추다 (have it tailored) and 교복이 어울리다 (it suits you). Its near-word 사복 (私服, 'private clothes') means your own casual clothes worn on non-uniform days — a 사복 데이 is a free-dress day. The English-speaker pitfall is treating Korean 'wear' as one word the way English does: English 'wear' covers shoes, hats, and shirts alike, but Korean splits them by body zone, so saying 교복을 신다 (using the shoe verb) is a telltale beginner slip — it must be 교복을 입다.

Using 쓰다 for the uniform after learning 모자를 쓰다 (wear a hat). 쓰다 is for things on the head; the uniform garment is 입다.

usage: 먹다 (eat) takes 를; 급식 is treated as the food you consume
맛있다 (tasty) with 가 is the universal verdict students pass on the food
급식 directly modifies 시간 to name the scheduled meal slot
the meal is served / comes out
나오다 describes today's menu 'coming out' on the tray
examples: 오늘 급식이 맛있어요.
Today's school meal is tasty.
The classic lunchroom line: 오늘 (today) plus subject 가 and 맛있다.
학생들이 급식을 먹으러 식당에 가요.
The students go to the cafeteria to eat lunch.
먹으러 (in order to eat) shows purpose with -(으)러; 를 marks 급식.
오늘 급식에 제가 제일 좋아하는 닭갈비가 나왔어요!
My favorite dak-galbi came out in today's school lunch!
An excited report: 급식에 ... 나오다 (appear in the meal); 에 marks the meal as where the dish shows up.
nuance: 급식 is the meal supplied institutionally — the school (or workplace) lunch served en masse and eaten together, usually on a divided tray (식판). The hanja 給食 is 給 (give/supply) + 食 (food/meal), literally 'supplied food', which captures that it is provided to a group rather than ordered individually. This is the dividing line from its near-words: 식사 (食事) is the formal/general word for 'a meal' (any meal, politely), 밥 is the casual everyday word for 'a meal' or 'rice', and 점심 names specifically 'lunch' by time of day — but only 급식 carries the sense of a meal institutionally provided to students/staff. So a meal you cook at home or buy at a restaurant is 밥 or 식사, never 급식; 급식 implies the cafeteria system. Natural phrases: 급식을 먹다 (eat it), 급식이 나오다 (today's menu is served), 급식 시간 (lunch period). The English-speaker pitfall is using 급식 for any lunch — if you ate lunch at a café you say 점심을 먹었어요 or 밥을 먹었어요, not 급식을 먹었어요, because 급식 specifically means the provided school/work meal.

Marking the served dish with 를 in 'a dish came out in the meal'. The dish appears via 나오다 (intransitive), so the meal is the location with 에: 급식에 불고기가 나왔어요.

usage: fees are 내다 (pay/hand over to an institution), never 사다 (buy)
price is judged with 비싸다/싸다 (expensive/cheap), with 가 marking the subject
오르다 (rise) is the verb for prices increasing; note the 르 irregular (올라요)
한 달 (one month) modifies 수업료 to specify the period being paid for
examples: 수업료가 비싸요.
The tuition is expensive.
A plain price judgment: subject 가 with 비싸다, the core way to call something pricey.
저는 매달 학원 수업료를 내요.
I pay the academy tuition every month.
매달 (every month) sets the frequency; 내다 takes 를 for the fee you hand over.
올해 등록금이랑 수업료가 또 올라서 부담이 커요.
With registration and tuition fees rising again this year, the burden is heavy.
A real worry: 오르다 (rise) plus 부담이 크다 (the burden is big), 등록금 vs 수업료 distinguished.
nuance: 수업료 is the fee charged for taking lessons — the money you pay an academy (학원), school, or course for instruction. The hanja 授業料 is 授 (give/confer) + 業 (work/study) — together 授業 means 'a lesson/class', the act of teaching being given — plus 料 (fee/charge), so literally 'lesson-fee'. The element 料 marks fees throughout Korean: 입장료 (admission), 수수료 (commission), 사용료 (usage fee), 수업료 (tuition). Distinguish it from the near-word 등록금 (登錄金, 'registration money'), the lump enrollment fee for a university semester — at a 대학교 you usually pay 등록금, while at a 학원 you pay 수업료 each month; many learners blur them. The essential verb is 내다 (수업료를 내다, to pay/remit a fee), and prices 오르다 (rise) or are 비싸다 (expensive). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 사다 (buy) because English can 'pay for' a class as if purchasing it — but in Korean you do not 'buy' a fee; you 내다 (pay/hand over) it: 수업료를 사다 is wrong, 수업료를 내다 is right.

Describing the fee with 커요 for 'high'. A price is 비싸다 (expensive), not 크다: 수업료가 비싸요. Reserve 크다 for physical size.

usage: 받다 (receive) takes 를; a scholarship is awarded to you
신청하다 (to apply/request) is the verb for putting in an application
나오다 describes the award money being granted/disbursed
타다 colloquially means to be awarded a prize or scholarship
examples: 장학금을 받았어요.
I got a scholarship.
The proud one-liner: 받다 plus past -았어요, 를 marking the award.
성적이 좋아서 이번 학기에 장학금을 신청했어요.
My grades were good, so I applied for a scholarship this term.
-아서 gives the reason (good grades); 신청하다 is the act of applying.
전액 장학금을 타서 등록금 걱정이 없어졌어요.
I won a full scholarship, so my tuition worries are gone.
전액 (full amount) modifies it; 타다 (win) plus the relief of 걱정이 없어지다.
nuance: 장학금 is the award money granted to a student to support their studies — for merit (성적 장학금), need, or special talent — money you do not repay, unlike a loan. The hanja 奬學金 is 奬 (encourage/reward) + 學 (study/learning) + 金 (money/gold), literally 'study-encouraging money', so the very word frames it as funds that reward and enable learning. Distinguish it sharply from 학자금 (學資金, 'study-capital'), which is the broader pool of money for education and often appears in 학자금 대출 (a student loan you must repay): a 장학금 is given to you, whereas 학자금 대출 is borrowed. Also unlike a plain 돈 (money) or 용돈 (allowance), 장학금 specifically denotes an academic award. The natural verbs are 장학금을 받다 (formally receive) and the colloquial 장학금을 타다 (win/get one), plus 장학금을 신청하다 (apply) and 장학금이 나오다 (it comes through). The English-speaker pitfall is calling it just 돈 — saying 학교에서 돈을 받았어요 to mean a scholarship loses the meaning; the award is 장학금, and confusing it with the repayable 학자금 대출 reverses who gives money to whom.

usage: 들어가다 (enter/go into) with 에 is the set phrase for joining a club
활동하다 (to be active/take part) happens at the club, so 에서
가입하다 (to enroll/become a member) is the more formal 'join'
the activity name (사진) modifies 동아리 directly to name the club's focus
examples: 저는 음악 동아리에 들어갔어요.
I joined a music club.
에 marks the club as what you entered (들어가다); past tense -았어요.
우리 동아리에서 매주 금요일에 모여요.
Our club meets every Friday.
에서 because 모이다 (the activity of gathering) takes place there; 매주 sets the rhythm.
동아리 활동 덕분에 선배들이랑 친해졌어요.
Thanks to club activities I got close with the older students.
덕분에 (thanks to) plus 친해지다 (grow close) — the real social payoff of joining.
nuance: 동아리 is a student club or society — a voluntary group bound by a shared hobby or interest (band, film, basketball, debate) that meets regularly, central to Korean school and university life. Unlike most school vocabulary here, it is a NATIVE Korean word, not Sino-Korean, which is why it has no hanja and a soft, homegrown feel. Distinguish it from its near-words: 동호회 (同好會) is the equivalent club for adults/the general public (a hiking 동호회, a tennis 동호회), 모임 is any informal gathering or get-together (a dinner 모임), and 클럽 the English loan tends to mean a nightclub or a formal organization — only 동아리 specifically names the student-interest club. The set verb is 동아리에 들어가다 (literally 'go into the club' = join) or the formal 가입하다, and you 동아리에서 활동하다 (are active in it), with 에서 marking the place of activity. The English-speaker pitfall is two-fold: using 모임 (a one-off gathering) for what is really an ongoing 동아리, and reaching for 참가하다/join with a wrong particle — Korean says 동아리에 들어가다 (에, destination of entering), not 동아리를 들어가다.

usage: 살다 (live/reside) takes 에 to mark the dwelling place
지내다 (to stay/get by) is an action over time, so the place takes 에서
들어가다 with 에 means to move in / take up residence there
기숙사 modifies 생활 (life) to name the experience of living in one
examples: 저는 기숙사에 살아요.
I live in the dormitory.
The basic residence statement: 살다 with the location particle 에.
기숙사에서 룸메이트랑 같이 지내요.
I'm staying in the dorm with a roommate.
에서 because 지내다 (the ongoing activity of living) happens there; 룸메이트랑 (with a roommate).
기숙사는 밤 11시에 통금이라서 일찍 들어가야 해요.
The dorm has an 11 p.m. curfew, so I have to go in early.
A real rule of dorm life: 통금 (curfew) plus -아야 하다 (have to); 들어가다 for going in.
nuance: 기숙사 is a dormitory — a residential building where students or workers live communally near their school or job, typically with shared rooms, rules, and a curfew (통금). The hanja 寄宿舍 is 寄 (lodge/entrust) + 宿 (stay overnight/lodge) + 舍 (house/building), literally a 'lodging house', a place you stay away from home. The 宿 element recurs in lodging words — 숙박 (宿泊, lodging), 합숙 (合宿, a training-camp stay), 숙소 (宿所, the place you stay) — all sharing 宿 'lodge / stay overnight'. Distinguish it from its near-words: 자취방 / 자취 is living alone off-campus in a rented room (자취하다, to live on one's own), 하숙 (下宿) is boarding with a family who provides meals, and 원룸 is a studio flat — only 기숙사 means the institution-run communal dorm. The dual-particle logic matters: use 에 for the state of residing (기숙사에 살다) and motion in (기숙사에 들어가다), but 에서 for activities done there (기숙사에서 공부하다/지내다). The English-speaker pitfall is calling it 집 (home) — your 기숙사 is where you stay, but 집 evokes your family home; a student says 기숙사에 가요 to go back to the dorm, while 집에 가요 means going to their actual home, often a different place entirely.
